confidence_note: Checked against book text (Preface and Final Thoughts). Old text dropped: "Marcus wanted to be a philosopher" (not in the book) and the plague-taught-human-nature chain. Replaced by the Avidius Cassius episode, which the book tells.
facts: Preface: year 170, night in tent on the Germania front, Marcus writes for himself; his reign brought near-constant war, plague, an attempt on his throne by a close ally, a depleted treasury, a greedy incompetent stepbrother as co-emperor.
Late in reign, sick and possibly near death, Marcus learned his old friend and most trusted general Avidius Cassius had rebelled in Syria and declared himself Caesar.
Marcus did nothing, kept the news from his troops, waited to see whether Cassius would come to his senses.

Cassius did not; Marcus told a council of soldiers they would march but the prize would be to capture him, to forgive a man who has wronged one; settle it well and show a right way to deal even with civil wars.
He sent troops to Rome to calm panicking crowds.
Three months later a lone assassin killed Cassius in Egypt; Marcus lost the chance to forgive in person but forgave more widely.
He refused to put coconspirators to death or prosecute senators and governors; he wrote asking the senate to keep his reign unstained by the blood of any senator.
Holiday: he controlled his perceptions, did not take it personally, then acted.
tension: A betrayed, sick emperor gets the revenge history would excuse and declines it.
opening_idea: Open on the secret kept from the troops.

lessons.idea: See what happened before you answer it.
lessons.anchor: Marcus waited and moved only once Cassius would not turn back.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A cafe owner learns a partner quietly left and writes down what happened and what the business needs before messaging.

reflect_final: If you waited a day before answering someone who you feel has wronged you, what would you do with that day?

use_cases.situation: A colleague went over your head.
use_cases.move: Say you will not answer in the heat of the moment.
Listen to yourself first, then ask what happened.

use_cases.situation: You are about to type an angry message.
use_cases.move: Keep it as a draft until tomorrow.

pocket_idea: Marcus waited when his general rebelled, then acted.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: When his general rebelled, Marcus Aurelius told his troops to capture him alive, and after the man was killed he forgave the conspirators.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Sick Marcus heard Cassius had declared himself Caesar in Syria, kept it from his troops, and waited. He marched to capture rather than kill; after an assassin killed Cassius he spared the coconspirators. Holiday: obstacle becomes the way.
